text:
UKRAINE. Donbas.
A plume of brown dust billows up from the wet, potholed dirt road as an armored personnel carrier (APC) rumbles into view. Its angular metal form, painted in military olive green, dwarfs the surrounding landscape. Soldiers, clad in combat fatigues, their faces obscured by beanies, peer out at the onlookers.

UKRAINE. Donbas.
A lone soldier stands guard in a frontline outpost. The parched earth stretches outward, a barren canvas marred only by the skeletal forms of drought-resistant shrubs clinging to life.

UKRAINE. Zaporizhzhia.
A single hole pierces the windshield, a spiderweb of cracks radiating outwards. Rainwater streams down, blurring the fractured world beyond. The circle with jagged edges leaves no doubt - shrapnel tore through the glass, a chilling reminder of the danger lurking outside and everywhere on the front line.

UKRAINE. Donbas.
A desolate Donbas frontline. A 105mm howitzer, cloaked in the smoke of a fired projectile, stands stark against a backdrop of skeletal trees, their barren branches reaching skyward. The ominous, chilling reality is the immense power unleashed in a war that scars the landscape.

UKRAINE. Kramatorsk. December 23, 2023.
A 40-year-old captured Russian soldier from Tver displayed signs of physical wear, including damaged fingernails. He stated he did not want to fight upon capture near Avdiivka days after deployment. The soldier's condition could be indicative of the harsh realities of war.

UKRAINE. Kramatorsk. December 23, 2023.
A 58-year-old captured Russian soldier, originally from St. Petersburg, claimed he was snapped by the Russian military on the street and assigned to an assault brigade in Siberia before deployment.

UKRAINE. Donbas.
An anti-tank defense system lies concealed behind a line of bare trees. The system incorporates dragon teeth and barbed wire, creating a physical barrier against potential armored vehicles.

UKRAINE. Zaporizhzhia.
A soldier finds respite in a leafless forest, the aftermath of an aborted task weighing on the stillness of the surroundings.

UKRAINE. Kramatorsk. December 23, 2023.
Three captured Russian soldiers, identified as prisoners of war (POWs), were taken near Avdiivka just days after their deployment with an assault brigade from Siberia.

UKRAINE. Zaporizhzhia.
Unyielding, the POW sat through the interview. His body remained taut, the only telltale signs of inner turmoil being a faint clench of his jaw and an occasional, subtle shift in posture.

UKRAINE. Donbas.
Deep within a dense forest in the front line, nestled amongst the leaves and fallen branches, lies a Ukrainian artillery outpost. Smoke curls from a chimney, hinting at the warmth and sustenance provided by a crackling
stove within.

UKRAINE. Kramatorsk. December 23, 2023.
Three captured Russian soldiers, identified as prisoners of war (POWs), reportedly unwilling to fight, were taken near Avdiivka just days after their deployment with an assault brigade from Siberia. A Ukrainian soldier, his hand resting on his AK rifle, guarded them closely.

UKRAINE. Donbas.
As the sun sets, military snipers conclude their practice and stow their rifles near a frontline post. The fading daylight casts eerie silhouettes of them and their rifles, underscoring the conclusion of the training session in an oddly subdued atmosphere.

UKRAINE. Kharkiv.
An inky black, circular cloud dominates the vast expanse of sky over the highway towards Kharkiv. Its swirling form casts a dramatic shadow, dwarfing the cars resembling minuscule insects traversing the road below. The stark contrast between the colossal cloud and the tiny vehicles underscores the immense power of nature.

pairs.head: Education and Work Experience
pairs.body:
Chang received a BA from Soochow University in Taipei and an MS from Indiana University, Bloomington.
He worked as a photojournalist at The Seattle Times and The Baltimore Sun. 
Chang joined Magnum Photos in 1995 and was elected as a Full Member in 2001. 
His photographic works have been widely published in internationally renowned media such as National Geographic, TIME magazine, New York Times and Der Spiegel.

pairs.head: Selected Exhibitions and Collections
pairs.body: Chang's works have been shown in galleries and museums around the world including Venice Biennale, São Paulo Biennial, International Center of Photography. His photographic works has been in the collection of Henri Cartier-Bresson Foundation, George Eastman Museum, International Center of Photography, Queens Museum, Taipei Fine Arts Museume, Chimei Museum, and National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts.

“No one asked whether we wanted to go. We got the order, and forward we went.”

These words come from a captured Russian lieutenant from the 71st Motorized Infantry Regiment, interviewed in Zaporizhia. Like countless others, his story reveals war's often unwanted realities.

The interview and photo session request received an unexpected positive response, particularly given the proximity to the front lines. The weight of the opportunity pressed down on me, and sleep remained elusive all night.

The stark contrast between anticipation and the reality of our meeting point was immediately apparent. By 10:00 AM, my fixer and I arrived at a lone gas station, seemingly untouched by time—a mid-sized, rusty, whitish bus squatted beside a weathered brick building. Peeling paint and boarded-up windows whispered tales of abandonment. Only the drooping gas nozzles, limp-like deflated balloons, and the cryptic numbers on the gauges remained a silent testament to the last fill-up, long gone.

Beyond the deserted outpost, a sun-scorched wasteland unfolded. A parched and uneven grass carpet extended outwards, interrupted only by the skeletal forms of shrubs clinging to life. An eerie silence, broken only by the wind's sigh, draped the surroundings.

Abruptly, the oppressive silence shattered. Ear-splitting screeches announced military vehicles, their swift blurs streaking across the horizon. These fleeting glimpses of raw power were a chilling reminder of unseen forces, further amplifying the abandoned station's disquiet. 

A white Toyota Corolla, a relic of the early 2000s, perched incongruously behind the rusty bus amidst the bleak landscape. Its tinted windows concealed the figures within, their presence fueling a prickle of unease in an already perplexing scene. 

Ten minutes later, a mud-caked black SUV bearing military plates rolled in. My fixer exchanged a curt greeting with the driver—a grim-faced man of medium build clad in an olive green jacket devoid of insignia save for a holstered pistol. His affiliation, be it Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (GUR) or Security Service (SBU), remained unanswered. We circled the dilapidated building, and as we passed the Toyota, a flicker of movement through the tinted windows offered a possible glance of the prisoner: a figure obscured by a beanie pulled low, the brim wrapped in blue tape. Yet, the changing light and tinted glass left the scene ambiguous.

Stepping inside the roughly 80 square meters building, I was confronted with dust and gloom—the enclosed space reeked of stale air and a faint mustiness. Peeling paint, roughly hewn beams, and cobwebbed cracks spoke of neglect. Rusty dividers and scattered straw littered the uneven floor—a bygone life, perhaps livestock. Slivers of light, filtering through boarded windows and a broken door, barely pierced the near-darkness.

Two car doors slammed shut. Moments later, a towering figure filled the doorway. The soldier, easily exceeding 1.9 meters and built like a bull with a thick beard, exuded a menacing aura. Armored and rifle-wielding, he shoved the masked captive into the dim space. His hands bound and eyes obscured, remained motionless until the soldier retrieved a weathered wooden box for him to sit. 

The stern soldier, beard a dark curtain, spoke in hushed tones to the grim-faced man. A swift flick of the wrist and a balaclava masked the soldier’s features and prevented prisoners of war from remembering his appearance, avoiding recognition or accusation in the future. With a brisk movement, he removed the blue tape from the captive's head and hands using his combat knife and pushed the cap up to his forehead, the metallic scrape echoing sharply in the near silence.

"The captive with the tape could have provided a full picture," I said with concern. "Surely, but we wouldn't want our captured soldiers in Russia to be subjected to such treatment," said my fixer. Later in the evening, however, I realized he had already snapped pictures with his phone of the captive with the tape and uploaded them to his Instagram Story!

While the Geneva Conventions, particularly the Third Convention on Prisoners of War (POW), don't explicitly forbid publishing a prisoner's name, they outline various safeguards concerning such a scenario.

“This is Chien-Chi Chang, a Taiwanese photojournalist.” My fixer facilitated the introduction. I briefly eyed the POW, who nodded and consented to the interview and photos. However, his name and face were withheld to protect his safety.

The young man, around 1.8 meters tall, displayed a youthful visage framed by handsome features. Instead of a POW camp’s blue uniform, he remained garbed in military uniform, the drab-blown camouflage fabric recently cleaned yet marked by the indelible reminders of the war. His voice, subdued and bordering on a whisper, prompted my fixer to adjust the phone recorder's proximity to capture his words. At one point, the absorbed soldier gestured bluntly, indicating a need for increased volume.

A sense of stillness permeated him throughout the interview, his form frozen in place except for the quiet play of his lips and the occasional flicker of eye contact.

Born in Istanbul and raised in Chechnya, the 22-year-old lieutenant found himself on a path seemingly preordained for military service, culminating in graduation from the Far East Higher Military Academy in Amur. However, the brutal realities of war soon shattered his preconceived notions.

Beyond the statistics and weariness etched on his face from the November 4, 2023 interview, the following month, I went on to photograph three POWs in Kramatorsk. This summary delves into the man's experience. I further went on to his own words (as paraphrased), revealing the man's raw emotions and viewpoints.

Fresh out of military school, they told him it was his duty. Orders were orders. War had broken out in Ukraine, and they needed officers. "There was only one road—to war," he remembered, the words catching in his throat. “No one asked whether we wanted to go. We got the order, and forward we went." This blind obedience, this forced march towards violence he did not want to be a part of, still haunts him.

They shipped him out in September to an outpost of the 71st Motorized Infantry Regiment. That was a muscular unit with 26 soldiers ready to defend. Their task was guarding a wooded area in the Rabotyne district (southeast of Zaporizhzhia.) It started with the equipment checks, and soon afterward, they evacuated, helping civilians escape the line of fire. A constant sense of unease was hanging heavy in the air because war had a way of twisting everything. They were supposed to be the defenders, but fear gnawed at them constantly. Artillery fire rained down. Tanks rumbled in the distance, a constant reminder of the firepower they faced. 

When asked what kind of weapons his unit was equipped with, he replied, “Machine guns, anti-tank weapons, and grenade launchers. We had tanks and artillery pieces. I don’t know how many of what (in the regiment) precisely.”

And drones, those buzzing things in the sky, were the stark reality in the sky watching their every move. “What the drones were aiming at was our first concern. Some are used for reconnaissance, others to relay coordinates for shelling. That’s what we were mostly concerned about. Regarding the FPV (first-person-view) drones, it was about who was quicker,” i.e., the drone or the target seeking cover. 

He mentioned that most of the time, they were hunkered down, waiting for the next attack. The camaraderie was a bond forged in fear and shared hardship. But it couldn't erase the gnawing feeling that any moment could be their last.

Additionally, he said half the guys didn't want to be there. Some were fighting for money, others for reasons he couldn't fathom. But the other half, like him, just wanted to go home.

This war has tentacles everywhere and is way messier than anyone thought. He said they bumped into Wagner Group soldiers in their area: “In my position, there was one. And in another position, there were two. The one at my position had fought in and around Bakhmut, and the other two Wagner PMC fighters had returned from Africa to fight in Ukraine for the first time.

Then there were the losses. They started with 26; only 12 were left when he was captured. Some fell to shelling, others to gunfire. As for the wounded, some made it, and some didn't. It all became a blur, a desperate fight for survival in a situation he never wanted.

Looking back, he blamed the leadership. They sent him and his comrades out with faulty intel, poor support, and a strategy that seemed more about throwing bodies at the problem than winning. It wasn't surprising that desertions started happening. He said that around 5% of each unit, guys just vanishing, choosing their fate over the one they were handed. Doubt started creeping in, too. There were whispers about the actual number of casualties of 350,000 to 400,000, and that victory might be a pipe dream. 

And then, he was captured. Surrounded, cut off from his unit. "You see," he said, bitterness creeping into his voice, "the fact that I am here is because of my commanders, who just abandoned me without the backing that allowed Ukrainians to encircle me." Now, he’s a prisoner of war with a heavy burden of what he’s seen and been through. War may be about duty but also about lives shattered and dreams buried. It's a harsh reality he never wanted to face.

His voice echoed in the silence as he recounted his ordeal. This summary aims to transport you there, but it's just one perspective on a vast conflict, a single shard, and a fragment chipped away from a monolithic narrative. The whole picture remains obscured, a tangled web woven from countless threads, each concealing a puzzle piece. Admittedly, the officially sanctioned prisoner exchanges might offer glimpses of the truth, but even then, uncertainty lingers. 

A crisp wind carrying the faint scent of decaying leaves signaled the approach of winter. Bare branches clawed at the leaden sky as the breeze rustled through them, creating a sound akin to brittle whispers. Meanwhile, the stoic soldiers had already secured the lieutenant's beanie with tape and bound his hands. Three car doors slammed shut in rapid succession. At precisely 10:30 AM, I witnessed the black SUV and the white Toyota dissolve into the distance, leaving behind a swirling plume of dust and a chilling sense of finality. This was not a departure but a disappearance, a scene ripped from a forgotten thriller.
